text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
The Spanish Monarch known as PHILIP the Handsome, PHILIP I, was born in 1478. His widow kept his mummified body in her room for several years. She was known as JOANNA the Mad.
German astronomer FRIEDRICH BESSELL, who worked out the orbit of Halley's Comet, was born in 1784. He was also the first to calculate the distance of a star from Earth.
Austrian monk and botanist GREGOR MENDEL, who discovered the laws of genetics by growing peas, was born in 1822.

The man who gave birth to "spoonerisms", Reverend WILLIAM SPOONER, was born in England in 1848. He was an albino, and his conversation was full of mixed-up words. As he would say, he lived in the age of "Queer Old Dean Victoria".
Australian cattle king MICHAEL DURACK was born in 1865. He fathered a dynasty of writers, artists and politicians.
Australian writer ALAN MOOREHEAD, who wrote 'Gallipoli', was born in Melbourne in 1910.

United States actor and singer BOBBY SHERMAN was born in 1945. He starred in many television programs such as 'Shindig', 'Here Come The Brides' and 'Getting Together'. His musical hits included "Little Woman" (1969), "La La La" (1969), "Easy Come, Easy Go" (1970) and "Julie, Do Ya Love Me" (1970). They were all million sellers.

Drummer, singer and songwriter with The Eagles, DON HENLEY, was born in 1947. He started his musical career in 1963 with the Four Speeds. In 1971 he was a member of LINDA RONSTADT's backing band, which became The Eagles that year. Hits included "Witchy Woman" (1972), "Best of My Love" (1974), "One of These Nights" (1975), "Lyin' Eyes" (1975), "Take it to the Limit" (1975), "New Kid in Town" (1976), "Hotel California" (1977), "Heartache Tonight" (1979) and "The Long Run" (1979). In 1981 the group announced it was splitting up and DON began a solo career. His hits have included "Leather and Lace" (1981), "All She Wants to do is Dance" (1985) and "The End of Innocence" (1989).
** EVENTS **
1456 : Hungarian general JANOS HUNYADI defeated the Turks
besieging Belgrade.
1739 : The Turks defeated troops of the Holy Roman Empire
at Crocyka, Yugoslavia, and threatened Belgrade.
1812 : The Duke of WELLINGTON defeated the French under
Marshal MARMONT at the battle of Salamanca.
1878: A tragic event in Australia's maritime history when
the three-masted iron barque, "James Service", struck Murray Reef south-west of Perth. The 24 people on board drowned. Many of them were performers en route from Calcutta to Melbourne.
1911: Two conservative forces, the Commonwealth Liberal
Party and the People's Party, united to form the People's Liberal Party.
1912: Australian swimmer, FANNY DURACK, became the first
Australian woman gold medallist at a modern Olympics by winning the 100 metres freestyle.
1933 : WILEY POST, U.S. pioneer aviator, became the first
person to fly solo around the world, in seven days 18 hours 49 minutes.
1934 : U.S. bank robber and public enemy number one JOHN
DILLINGER was shot dead by FBI agents outside Chicago's Biograph Theatre after 13 months on the run.
1938: In Germany, Jews were forced to carry special
identity cards.
1946: Britons faced their first day of bread-rationing
after the end of World War II. The extension of rationing was due to a poor harvest, droughts and shortages in fertilizers.
1952: The first Australian woman to win a track gold
medal, MARJORIE JACKSON, won the 100 metres at the Helsinki Olympic Games.
1957: BP and Shell decided to quit Israel under pressure
from Arab Oil producers.
1968: The discovery of Aboriginal bones at Lake Mungo in
New South Wales proved that Aborigines lived in Australia at least 25,000 years ago.
1969: Apollo 11 left the Moon after the historic first
human moon walk.
1970: Australia's RAELENE BOYLE was the women's sprint
star of the Commonwealth Games in Edinburgh, after winning her second gold medal. She won the 100 and 200 metres.
1972 : The European Economic Community (EEC) and European
Free Trade Area (EFTA) agreed on a new free trade area linking the two organisations, effective January 1, 1973.
1973: The French tested an H-bomb near Mururoa Atoll in

the South Pacific. The explosion, the first in a new series of atmospheric nuclear test, went ahead despite the presence of the New Zealand protest frigate 'Otago' within the French-declared danger zone.
1975: The ACTU (Australian Council of Trade Unions)
entered the cut-price petrol business with its 'Solo' service stations.
1979: Australia agreed to lift its intake of Indo-Chinese
refugees to 14,000 over the next year. This represented a three-fold increase.
1983: Australian adventurer DICK SMITH completed the
first round-the-world solo helicopter flight.
1988: Two of Australia's most wanted men, RUSSELL "MAD
DOG" COX and RAYMOND DENNING, were captured in a supermarket car park in Melbourne. The two had escaped from New South Wales' jails where they were serving life sentences.
1992: Colombian drug lord PABLO ESCOBAR escaped from
prison. The jail was minimum security and full of luxuries for ESCOBAR, but he broke out after hearing that he was to be transfered to a more secure and less lavish institution.
1984: The event known as "The Paddington Bear Affair" saw

Australia's Special Minister of State, MICK YOUNG, criticised for failing to declare that he was bringing 'Paddington' into the country. Mr YOUNG admitted he made a false declaration to customs about luggage he brought into Australia from London. He failed to declare gifts worth more than $700 and therefore evaded more than $600 in duty and sales tax. Mr YOUNG, who said he didn't know what was in the baggage, stood down until an inquiry found "no impropriety" in the case.
1993 : Japanese Prime Minister KIICHI MIYAZAWA resigned
as president of the Liberal Democratic Party, taking the blame for party's worst-ever election performance.
1995 : HAROLD LARWOOD, English fast bowler, died. He
spearheaded the attack on Australia's batsmen in the notorious "bodyline" cricket series of the early 1930s.
